Valley
VAL-ē
n. (rendering Hebrew 'ēmeq, gay', biq'âh, nachal, and Greek pharanx)
From Old French valee, from Latin vallis. The Hebrew is much richer than the English and distinguishes at least four things the Authorized Version renders alike: 'ēmeq, the broad open vale; gay', the narrow steep-sided ravine (the word in the valley of the son of Hinnom, whence Gehenna); biq'âh, a wide plain between mountains (the valley of dry bones); and nachal, a wadi, a torrent-bed dry for most of the year and dangerous in the rains.

Biblical Definition

In the geography of Scripture the valley is where the decisive things happen. It is the place of battle — the valley of Elah where David met Goliath, the valley of Jehoshaphat, the valley of Megiddo — because armies meet on level ground between the hills. It is the place of idolatry and judgment, since the valley of the son of Hinnom, where children were made to pass through the fire, gave its name to Gehenna, the standing New Testament word for hell. It is the place of vision and resurrection: the hand of the LORD set Ezekiel down “in the midst of the valley which was full of bones” (Eze 37:1), and there the question was asked whether these bones could live. It is the place of decision under the day of the LORD — “Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision” (Joe 3:14). Above all it is the shepherd's figure for the darkest passage of the believer's life: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me” (Psa 23:4). The preposition governs the comfort — through, not into; it is a passage and not a residence, and the presence of the shepherd rather than the absence of the shadow is what removes the fear. The prophetic reversal completes the theme: at the coming of the LORD “every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low” (Isa 40:4), the low places raised and the high brought down, which is the geography of grace stated as a landscape.

Webster 1828 Definition

The low ground between hills; in Scripture the place of battle, of idolatrous fire, of the vision of dry bones and of decision under the day of the LORD, and, in the twenty-third psalm, the shadowed passage walked through rather than dwelt in, with the shepherd present.

VALLEY, n. 1. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.

2. In Scripture, the Hebrew has several words rendered by this one; the broad vale, the narrow ravine, the plain between mountains, and the torrent bed which is dry in summer.

3. The valley of the shadow of death; the darkest and most perilous passage of life, and by usage the approach of death itself. Psalm 23.

4. The valley of the son of Hinnom, or Tophet, where the idolatrous Israelites burnt their children to Molech, and which afterwards became the receptacle of the filth of the city; whence Gehenna, the word for hell. 2 Kings 23; Jer. 7.

5. The valley of decision; the place of judgment in the day of the LORD. Joel 3.

Key Scripture

Psalm 23:4 — "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."

Ezekiel 37:1 — "The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones,"

Joel 3:14 — "Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision."

Isaiah 40:4 — "Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:"

Modern Corruption

The valley of the shadow of death is softened into a metaphor for a difficult season and emptied of both death and the shepherd, so that a psalm about dying in company becomes a sentiment about coping alone.

expand to see more

Psa 23:4 is the most quoted verse in the psalter and among the least attended. Two things are commonly lost. The first is death: the phrase is regularly applied to any hardship whatever, until the psalm no longer speaks to the one thing it was written to carry a man through. The second is the change of person. Through the first three verses David speaks of the shepherd in the third person — he maketh, he leadeth, he restoreth — and precisely at the valley he turns and speaks to Him: for thou art with me. The comfort of the psalm is not a proposition about God but the presence of God addressed directly, and it arrives exactly where the light fails. A reading that keeps the imagery and drops the Person has kept the wrapping.

The rod and the staff are the other casualty. Modern sentiment hears them as gentle accessories; they are a club and a crook, the one for beating off predators and the other for hooking a sheep out of a place it should not have gone. They comfort because they are instruments of force used on the sheep's behalf and, when needed, on the sheep. This is the same God who says that whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth. A shepherd who carried nothing would be no comfort at all in a ravine, and a God who never disciplined would be no Father.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew distinguishes the broad vale ('ēmeq), the steep ravine (gay'), the plain among mountains (biq'âh), and the seasonal torrent bed (nachal). Greek pharanx renders the term in Luke's quotation of Isaiah.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ēmeq (H6010) — a broad open valley or vale; the valley of Elah, the valley of Achor, the valley of Jehoshaphat.

Hebrew gay' (H1516) — a narrow steep-sided ravine; the word in the valley of the son of Hinnom and in the valley of the shadow of death (Psa 23:4).

Hebrew biq'âh (H1237) — a wide plain between mountains, from bāqa', to cleave; the plain of Shinar and the valley full of bones (Eze 37:1).

Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent bed or wadi, dry in summer and flooding in the rains; the brook Kidron, the brook Cherith where Elijah was fed.

Greek pharanx (G5327) — a ravine, a valley; used in Luk 3:5, every valley shall be filled, quoting Isa 40:4 of the Baptist's ministry.

Usage

"Of battle and decision: the valley of Elah (1Sa 17:2); multitudes in the valley of decision (Joe 3:14)."

"Of judgment and idolatry: the valley of the son of Hinnom, Tophet (Jer 7:31-32), from which Gehenna takes its name."

"Of the believer's dark passage and its reversal: through the valley of the shadow of death (Psa 23:4); every valley shall be exalted (Isa 40:4)."
